waverly_match_codes.3117: 1928 garage/showroom on a livery site, ~7,000 sq ft

waverly_match_codes.3026: end-of-row house with porch, 1,555 sq ft

buildings.name: R. House
buildings.orig_use: Car showroom and garage.
buildings.new_use: Food hall with 10 stalls, a pop-up chef stall, a cocktail bar and event space, plus offices and a yoga studio in the same building.
buildings.financing: $12M-$13M (sources differ), part of the developer's $80M Remington Row project; no incentives stated.
buildings.outcome: Opened in Dec 2016 with its roll-up garage doors kept; no 2025-26 status found.
buildings.lesson: A curated food hall needed about 50,000 sq ft and a $12M+ developer, far too big for 3117, but a 2-3 stall version with pop-up testing could transfer.

buildings.name: Motor House
buildings.orig_use: Showroom of Baltimore's first Ford dealer, later other car dealers, an office-furniture store and an informal arts centre.
buildings.new_use: Arts hub with galleries, a black box theatre, nonprofit offices, artist studios and a bar and event room.
buildings.financing: $6.5M including purchase, from tax credits, grants and a state bond bill; foundation support.
buildings.outcome: Operating and marking its 10th year in 2025; it reopened days after a car crashed through the front doors in June 2025.
buildings.lesson: Closest match for 3117: eight years of informal low-cost arts use came before a nonprofit bought it and filled it with anchor nonprofit tenants, studios and a venue.

buildings.name: Open Works
buildings.orig_use: Original use unknown; past uses included a mechanic shop and a thrift store.
buildings.new_use: Public makerspace with wood, metal, digital and textile shops, rentable micro-studios and classes.
buildings.financing: $11.5M (or $11M) from bank investment, low-interest loans, a construction loan, and state and foundation grants.
buildings.outcome: Opened Sept 2016 at 1400 Greenmount Ave with memberships at $70-$125 a month; later status not verified.
buildings.lesson: A former mechanic shop on Greenmount Ave was paid for with a blended stack of loans, bank money and state and foundation grants, a route open to Waverly at smaller scale.

buildings.name: Superior Motors
buildings.orig_use: One of the first indoor car dealerships in the US.
buildings.new_use: Chef-led fine-dining restaurant that trained and hired residents and offered neighbours discounted meals.
buildings.financing: Over $250,000 from Kickstarter, local foundation money, and over $190,000 in pandemic PPP loans.
buildings.outcome: Closed at the start of the pandemic in 2020 and never reopened; in 2024 a local brewery announced a new restaurant for the space.
buildings.lesson: A destination restaurant built around one star chef was fragile in a very poor town; re-letting to a rooted local business is the lower-risk model.

buildings.name: Studio Theatre
buildings.orig_use: Car showroom on DC's 14th Street auto row (one source says Studio began in a former hot dog warehouse).
buildings.new_use: Four-stage nonprofit theatre complex, none over 225 seats, with a ground-floor cafe added in 2022.
buildings.financing: Leased in 1987, bought in 1997; a $20M renovation in 2022 drew $3.8M from the DC Arts Commission plus bank financing.
buildings.outcome: Grew into three adjoining buildings and reopened in 2022 after a $20M renovation.
buildings.lesson: Cheap empty showrooms on a declining auto row became a theatre cluster; leasing first and buying a decade later is a realistic path for a rent-free group at 3117.

sources.l: HMdb Logan Circle heritage marker, undated
Studio Theatre mission and history, undated

buildings.name: The Livery
buildings.orig_use: The Palace Livery, a horse livery stable.
buildings.new_use: Microbrewery and brewpub with live music.
buildings.outcome: In its 12th year in 2017 and billed as the county's oldest craft brewery; a former bartender and brewer later bought it.
buildings.lesson: A downtown-revival group restored a livery and then sold to an insider who knew the business; 3117's livery-site history is branding a food or drink operator can use.

buildings.name: SNF Parkway Theatre
buildings.orig_use: Vaudeville and movie house, later the Five West and a home for African-American film programming.
buildings.new_use: Three-screen nonprofit film centre (422 seats plus two 100-seat rooms) and home of the Maryland Film Festival.
buildings.financing: $18.5M; the city sold it and three lots for $1 (appraised about $1.2M); $5M from the Stavros Niarchos Foundation via JHU.
buildings.outcome: Closed in early 2023 when paid attendance fell to about 10,000 from 34,000 in 2019; relaunched in 2024 with mixed programming and hosted the 2025 festival.
buildings.lesson: Even a well-funded single-purpose cinema nearly failed on film tickets alone, so a 692-seat Waverly Theatre should plan for live, community and rental use from the start.

buildings.name: Creative Alliance at the Patterson
buildings.orig_use: Neighbourhood movie theatre, later split into two discount cinemas, closed in 1995.
buildings.new_use: Arts centre with a 200-seat flexible theatre, a 2,000 sq ft gallery, artist studios, classrooms and a cafe.
buildings.financing: Multi-million dollar project; a $7.5M 1998 HUD grant is reported only by a user-edited site; a $35K foundation operating grant in 2017.
buildings.outcome: Has run for over 20 years; in 2017 it planned to reuse another empty Eastern Ave building as an arts education centre.
buildings.lesson: The most transferable model for 3211: cut the house to a 200-seat flexible room and fill the rest with studios, a gallery and a cafe.

buildings.name: Carver Theater
buildings.orig_use: Segregation-era movie house for Black audiences, later a medical clinic.
buildings.new_use: Concert, event and entertainment hall with jazz, blues and brass nights.
buildings.financing: About $8M from federal New Markets and historic tax credits, state historic and live-performance credits, and state community development funds.
buildings.outcome: Listed for sale in 2016 and closed suddenly in Nov 2017 after losing its credit line; running events again by 2025 and put up for auction in July 2025 (result unknown).
buildings.lesson: A tax-credit-heavy theatre that fought downtown venues for touring acts lost its credit line within three years; 3211 should not compete with the city's big venues.

buildings.name: Capitol Theatre, Gordon Square
buildings.orig_use: Silent-movie house of about 1,400 seats in the Gordon Square Arcade.
buildings.new_use: Three-screen digital cinema showing first-run, independent and classic films.
buildings.financing: About $7.5M, made possible by federal New Markets Tax Credits; an earlier federal grant paid for the roof; a 2017 gala raised $70K for repairs.
buildings.outcome: Open with about 50,000-60,000 patrons a year, but the owner says screens alone do not cover building upkeep.
buildings.lesson: A CDC owner with a professional cinema chain as operator, financed with New Markets credits, kept a neighbourhood cinema running for 15+ years.

buildings.name: Uptown Theater
buildings.orig_use: Art Deco movie and stage theatre, a major venue for Black performers and civil-rights shows.
buildings.new_use: Planned community performing-arts centre with youth programmes, a tech centre and studios; a community radio station broadcasts from it.
buildings.financing: $14M budget never fully raised; state grants of $500K (2018) and $750K (2019).
buildings.outcome: Dark since 1978; reopening targets of 2017, 2019 and 2022 were missed, the founder died in 2020, and in 2024 the owner was talking to a new developer.
buildings.lesson: A small founder-led nonprofit chasing a $14M full restoration can stay dark for decades; phased interim use and a capable partner matter more for 3211.

buildings.name: Stony Island Arts Bank
buildings.orig_use: Stony Island Trust & Savings Bank, a bank until the 1980s.
buildings.new_use: Arts centre with exhibitions, archives of Black publishing and lantern slides, a library and events.
buildings.financing: Bought from the city for $1 in 2012; $4.5M renovation; later a $3.5M Mellon grant for collections.
buildings.outcome: Opened Oct 2015 after about 30 years empty and won a 2016 rehabilitation award; no 2025-26 status found.
buildings.lesson: A $1 purchase, a partial as-found restoration and a well-networked artist-operator turned a bank slated for demolition into an anchor, like 3117's repairs-only offer.

buildings.name: Currency Exchange Cafe / Retreat
buildings.orig_use: Run-down former currency exchange (check-cashing storefront).
buildings.new_use: Cafe, later a coffee house and training incubator for food and hospitality entrepreneurs with a chef in residence.
buildings.outcome: Reworked as 'Retreat' and operating from July 2021; events listed in April 2023; 2025-26 status unknown.
buildings.lesson: Turning a marginal storefront cafe into a training incubator made it a fundable workforce programme, a model for Waverly's 900-1,300 sq ft shops.

buildings.name: The Commons
buildings.orig_use: Former furniture shop on a once-busy Mack Avenue strip.
buildings.new_use: Laundromat, low-price coffee shop and community meeting space.
buildings.financing: Bought for $500 at a 2011 tax-foreclosure auction; about $1.5M of renovation from foundation grants and fundraising.
buildings.outcome: Soft-opened in March 2018 after years of resident meetings in a ZIP with about 50% building vacancy; later status not verified.
buildings.lesson: Pairing a daily need (a laundromat) with a cheap cafe brings existing low-income residents in every day, and residents picked the uses.

buildings.name: Anacostia Arts Center
buildings.orig_use: Three adjoining buildings leased to Woolworth's for most of the 20th century.
buildings.new_use: Black box theatre, studios for gallery, retail or yoga, a cafe, and a small-business incubator and coworking space.
buildings.financing: A local nonprofit bought the site in 1999 with a 15-year bank loan; a CDFI bought it in 2021; 500 sq ft rents for $1,399 a month with utilities, about half of market (2024).
buildings.outcome: Operating with food and retail tenants in 2024; joined a $500K bank-funded retail incubation pilot with new tenants in Oct 2026.
buildings.lesson: A former chain-store building on a majority-Black main street lasted once a mission lender owned it and rented at about half of market with business help.

sources.l: Anacostia Arts Center building history, undated

buildings.name: Cafe Hon
buildings.new_use: Kitschy neighbourhood diner and cafe, the origin of HONfest.
buildings.outcome: Closed in April 2022 after 30 years and was leased to a restaurant group; the owner's attempt to trademark 'Hon' caused a long community dispute.
buildings.lesson: One owner-run cafe can anchor a corridor's turnaround for decades, but cashing in on shared local identity draws backlash.

buildings.name: Red Canoe Bookstore Cafe
buildings.new_use: Children's bookstore and cafe on Harford Road.
buildings.outcome: Closed quietly in early 2024 after about 20 years and was re-let by late May to a boutique and tea lounge with a plant shop.
buildings.lesson: On a Baltimore Main Street like Waverly's, small shops close at owner life events rather than market failure, and a Main Street group re-let the space within months.

buildings.name: St. Roch Market
buildings.orig_use: Open-air seafood and public market.
buildings.new_use: Food hall of 12-13 vendor stalls that also works as a vendor incubator.
buildings.financing: $3.6M of public disaster-recovery money; the operator now holds a 30-year city lease and vendors pay rent or 30% of gross sales.
buildings.outcome: Vandalised as a symbol of gentrification weeks after opening and near closing by 2023; under an original vendor all 12 stalls were full with a waiting list in Oct 2024.
buildings.lesson: An upscale food hall in a public building on a poor, majority-Black corridor drew backlash and nearly failed; it recovered under an insider operator with revenue-share rents.

buildings.name: Eddie's Sweet Shop
buildings.orig_use: Ice-cream parlour and soda fountain since 1925 (a continuity case, not a conversion).
buildings.new_use: Same use with its period interior intact, serving 18 flavours from original recipes.
buildings.outcome: Open as of June 2025 and run by the same family since 1968.
buildings.lesson: For 3107's 1937 ice-cream parlour, an intact or recreated period interior is the brand, so restoring the fittings can be the business plan.

sources.l: Untapped New York, URL 2023-01-18, content June 2025

buildings.name: Nitehawk Prospect Park
buildings.orig_use: The Sanders Theatre, a single-screen neighbourhood cinema with 1,581 seats.
buildings.new_use: Dine-in cinema with 7 screens (650 seats in all), table service and two bars.
buildings.financing: Investors bought it for $28M in 2016 and leased it to the cinema operator; renovation cost unknown.
buildings.outcome: Operating; the house had city approval for condos in 2015 before that plan was dropped.
buildings.lesson: Split a big house into a few small screens and earn from food and drink; historic-district status helped keep it a cinema.

buildings.name: Spectacle Theater
buildings.orig_use: Bodega (corner grocery).
buildings.new_use: Volunteer-run 30-35 seat microcinema showing repertory, cult and experimental films.
buildings.financing: Mainly donations and a long-sighted rental deal; a 2015 Kickstarter covered a rent rise and required lease work.
buildings.outcome: Still running in Jan 2021, when it streamed during the pandemic; 2025-26 status not verified.
buildings.lesson: A grocery storefront can hold a 30-seat cinema with little build-out and volunteer staff; lease renewal is the main risk.

sources.l: Museum of Arts and Design press release, 2014-07-23

buildings.name: Berg'n (1000 Dean Street)
buildings.orig_use: Studebaker service station and warehouse with garage doors.
buildings.new_use: 400-seat beer hall with four food-vendor stalls, anchoring a creative-office conversion of the complex.
buildings.financing: Complex bought for about $11M plus about $30M of redevelopment; under contract for about $60M in 2019; offices asked $20-35/sq ft.
buildings.outcome: The beer hall helped the complex reach about 95% occupancy before its 2019 sale; Berg'n is now listed as closed (date and reason unknown).
buildings.lesson: A food and beer hall on a garage floor can anchor a big former auto building, but the value went to the owners, so a deal for 3117 should say who keeps the upside.

buildings.name: Pete's Candy Store
buildings.orig_use: Family luncheonette and candy store with fountain sodas.
buildings.new_use: Small bar with nightly free live music, readings, trivia and comedy in a tiny back room.
buildings.financing: Long lease at $800 a month in 1999; sources differ on whether the founder now owns the building.
buildings.outcome: Marked 25 years in Dec 2024, and the owner plans to keep it unchanged.
buildings.lesson: Keeping the old shop's name and fittings, plus a cheap long lease signed when the street was 'desolate', made a 25-year anchor.

buildings.name: JM Cafe, White Pagoda Temple
buildings.new_use: Coffee and bakery shop in a one-storey hutong building, with a sheltered front seating zone and a public roof terrace facing the White Pagoda.
buildings.outcome: Built June-Sept 2024 inside the state-led Baitasi renewal; only design-press coverage found.
buildings.lesson: A shop the size of Waverly's storefronts became a destination by adding a roof terrace and sheltered seating that face a landmark.

sources.l: mooool, 'JM Cafe, Baitasi branch / B.L.U.E. Architecture Studio' (in Chinese), c. 2025-03
ArchDaily project 1028109 (not fetched; URL as given in notes)

buildings.name: HAGISO
buildings.orig_use: Two-storey wooden apartment building, described as a temple-run boarding house.
buildings.new_use: Cafe, gallery, rental salon, design shop, and front desk for a hotel whose rooms are spread around the neighbourhood.
buildings.outcome: Saved from demolition after a three-week student exhibition drew about 1,500 visitors; it reached 10 years in 2023 and spread to more buildings.
buildings.lesson: A short free event inside an empty building is a cheap way to prove demand to a sceptical owner.

sources.l: Tokyo Treasure Islands, 'Field report: Yanesen course' (in Japanese), 2018-10-24

buildings.name: Ueno Sakuragi Atari
buildings.orig_use: Three traditional wooden rental houses whose elderly residents had moved out.
buildings.new_use: Craft beer hall, Norwegian bakery, and an oil, salt and sake shop around a shared courtyard.
buildings.financing: No public subsidy; the operator screened about 15 applicants to pick complementary tenants.
buildings.outcome: Operating as of 2022; a local NPO sparked the idea and a local builder did the work, with one fire alarm system linking the three houses.
buildings.lesson: Closest match for 3107: split a small property among three complementary tenants around a shared yard, without subsidy.

sources.l: UR Urban Renaissance Agency, 'Machimichi' newsletter No. 19 (in Japanese), 2017-03

buildings.name: Nui. Hostel & Bar Lounge
buildings.orig_use: Storage warehouse of a toy company.
buildings.new_use: Hostel with a ground-floor cafe, bar and lounge open to non-guests.
buildings.outcome: Opened Sept 2012 after a four-month renovation; the official site is live but current status is not verified.
buildings.lesson: A tall-ceilinged storage floor became a lounge where travellers and locals mix, so a big ground floor can be public day and night without a food-hall operator.

buildings.name: The Castle Cinema
buildings.orig_use: Castle Electric Theatre, a 619-seat cinema (1913-1958), later a glass factory, bingo hall, snooker club and shops.
buildings.new_use: Two-screen independent cinema (82 and 27 seats) with a bar and restaurant for up to 120.
buildings.financing: A 2016 Kickstarter raised GBP 57,000 from 650+ backers; a national film recovery grant followed in 2021.
buildings.outcome: Closed for COVID in 2020, reopened in May 2021 with recovery funding, and was operating as of 2023.
buildings.lesson: You don't need to restore all 692 seats: an 80-seat screen plus a bar in part of the old house, crowdfunded by locals, reopened a long-lost cinema.

buildings.name: Peckham Levels
buildings.orig_use: Council multi-storey car park.
buildings.new_use: Creative workspace with 50 studios, small offices, coworking, maker equipment, rehearsal rooms, yoga, events, shops and food outlets.
buildings.financing: Council-owned with a curator as master tenant; 20% of studios at about one-third of market rent and 10% of profits to a community fund.
buildings.outcome: Supported 450+ jobs with 67% of office tenants local; a 5,000-signature petition won a longer lease and events still ran in 2025.
buildings.lesson: Community duties written into the master lease (local share, cheap studios, volunteer hours, profit share) are a concrete template for 3117.

buildings.name: Brixton Village (Granville Arcade)
buildings.orig_use: Covered shopping arcade of 100+ small shops.
buildings.new_use: Indoor market of small food shops, boutiques, galleries and community shops; many units became cafes and restaurants after 2011.
buildings.financing: Thirty of 98 proposals got three months' free rent, with seed money from the landlord.
buildings.outcome: Fully let within months for the first time in 30 years, then pioneers were priced out after a 2018 sale; in 2026 it was pitched to private equity and traders began a GBP 15m buy-back bid.
buildings.lesson: Free-rent pop-ups filled long vacancies fast, but with no tenure or stake the value went to the next buyer, so tenure or a purchase option must come at the start.

buildings.name: De Hallen
buildings.orig_use: Depot for garaging and repairing the city's first electric trams.
buildings.new_use: Cultural hall with a 9-screen cinema, public library, food hall, hotel, TV studios and job-training workshops.
buildings.outcome: Squatted in 2010 after years empty and saved by neighbours and squatters; officially opened in 2015 and won a 2015 European heritage award.
buildings.lesson: Putting a library and job-training workshops beside the food hall and cinema keeps an old vehicle building useful to lower-income neighbours, not only visitors.

buildings.name: Blue House Cluster
buildings.orig_use: Shophouses with flats above and ground-floor shops (1920s-1950s).
buildings.new_use: Original residents stay; empty flats go to new co-living tenants who must join community activities, plus community and heritage uses.
buildings.financing: Government heritage partnership scheme; amounts unknown.
buildings.outcome: Won a 2017 UNESCO Asia-Pacific award as the first Hong Kong project where original residents stayed through and after the works; 11 new tenants joined.
buildings.lesson: Renovating with residents in place and asking newcomers to join community life avoids the empty bought-out house problem.

sources.l: Think City Institute, UNESCO Blue House summary, uploaded 2020-12

districts.name: The Avenue (W 36th St), Hampden
districts.stock: Four-block main street in 19th-century mill-village fabric; exact building ages unknown.
districts.historic: National Register district (2004 state registration cited); exact listing unknown.
districts.lead: Private entrepreneurs, artists and merchants from the early 1990s; no CDC or anchor led it.
districts.outcomes: Boutiques, restaurants and galleries filled empty shops and home prices soared; HonFest draws about 50,000 people over two days and the street resisted chains.
districts.displacement_note: Cultural displacement of working-class residents and a 2010-11 fight over the 'Hon' trademark; it stayed mostly white; no anti-displacement steps documented.
districts.lesson: A market-led revival of a similar small main street filled storefronts but is a poor equity model for Waverly.
districts.similarity: Low on demographics and process; high on physical form and the same JHU catchment.

districts.name: Eastern Avenue, Highlandtown
districts.stock: Ten blocks of rowhouse-scale shops plus big former anchors (two theatres and Haussner's); a state Arts & Entertainment District.
districts.anchor_institution: No university; cultural anchors are Creative Alliance and the Southeast Anchor Library.
districts.lead: Southeast CDC (founded 1975) and Highlandtown Main Street, with a community foundation and a private developer for the anchor site.
districts.outcomes: Building vacancy fell from 30% to 9% in about 10 years to 2017; home sale values rose 30% in one year (2017).
districts.vacancy_change: 30% to 9% building vacancy, c.2007-2017 (magazine figure, not primary data).
districts.displacement_note: Explicit goal of growing 'without leaving anyone behind' (home loans, eviction counselling, diverse boards); the 30% price jump signals pressure; nothing measured.
districts.lesson: The clearest Baltimore case of vacancy falling from 30% to 9% under a CDC-run Main Street, about 10 years after arts and anchor conversions.
districts.similarity: Medium: same 1970s urban renewal limits, rowhouse form and empty anchors, but an immigrant Latino base and no university.

sources.l: Southeast CDC Highlandtown Main Street, accessed 2026-10-19

districts.name: Harford Road, Hamilton-Lauraville
districts.stock: Streetcar-era strip of small 500-1,500 sq ft shops, plus the old firehouse and the historic Markley Hotel.
districts.lead: Hamilton-Lauraville Main Street, its director and merchant board, with local investors.
districts.outcomes: In FY2011 10 businesses opened and 6 closed for a net gain of 28 jobs; the firehouse was bought for $64,900 raised in two days and its incubator still runs in 2026.
districts.displacement_note: None documented; the model is built around local ownership.
districts.lesson: A community-financed building with a cheap incubator that feeds tenants into nearby empty shops is a low-cost answer to clustered vacancy.
districts.similarity: Medium on corridor type; demographics not verified.

districts.name: Washington Boulevard, Pigtown
districts.anchor_institution: Nearby university campus (UMB) and stadiums, which did not bring storefront demand.
districts.lead: The city's development agency as land assembler, private developers and Pigtown Main Street.
districts.outcomes: A 2006-09 developer deal on city-assembled shops failed when income could not cover debt, costs rose about 20% and banks would not lend; c.2021 residents still wanted more businesses.
districts.displacement_note: None documented; residents disagree on the wanted business mix. Median household income was $58,496 in 2019.
districts.lesson: Buying storefronts is not enough if each building's numbers don't work and lenders won't finance small mixed-use rehabs.
districts.similarity: High: mixed or majority-Black, moderate-to-low income rowhouse main street near anchors.

sources.l: Baltimore Sun via Yahoo, c. mid-2021

districts.name: Belair Road, Belair-Edison
districts.stock: About eight blocks on Belair Rd and Erdman Ave, including seven adjoining buildings at 3201-3215 Belair Rd.
districts.lead: Belair-Edison Neighborhoods Inc., a housing-focused CDC that runs the Main Street.
districts.outcomes: A 2018 state storefront grant redid signs, lighting and paint on seven adjoining buildings in five months; no outcomes reported.
districts.lesson: A current Baltimore Main Street peer, but the record is too thin for a numeric comparison.
districts.similarity: Probably high on demographics and corridor type, but unverified.

districts.name: Livernois Avenue of Fashion and Live6 (McNichols)
districts.stock: 1920s-1950s commercial blocks, including a former department store; surface parking was a third of frontage lots.
districts.anchor_institution: University of Detroit Mercy and Marygrove College, with the Kresge Foundation, through the Live6 Alliance.
districts.lead: City of Detroit and its development agency, the Live6 Alliance, merchant associations and a CDFI-type lender.
districts.outcomes: The $17M streetscape (2019-20) cut sales: one shop lost 33%, two businesses closed and 18 planned openings never happened; new shops and restaurants opened after 2020 (no count).
districts.displacement_note: No measured displacement; the main harm was business loss during construction, partly offset by $5k-$20k forgivable loans.
districts.lesson: An anchor-plus-foundation intermediary and a lender-owned low-rent retail building transfer well; phase street works so they don't stall openings.
districts.similarity: High: historically Black business district next to university anchors with a long-lived merchant group.

sources.l: City of Detroit Public Realm Plan, c. 2017

districts.name: 53rd Street and Harper Court, Hyde Park
districts.stock: Harper Court shops from 1965-70s with 23 stores in 2008; the new Harper Court (2013) is 223,775 sq ft with an office tower and hotel.
districts.anchor_institution: University of Chicago (owner, landlord and master developer).
districts.lead: University of Chicago as owner and master developer, with the city's tax-increment district, aldermen and developers.
districts.outcomes: Bought for $6.5M in 2008, rebuilt by 2013 with about 500 university staff moved in, and 100% leased by Dec 2017; a 2019 block party drew 50,000 people.
districts.vacancy_change: Harper Court fully leased by Dec 2017.
districts.displacement_note: 17 Harper Court tenants, including Black-owned restaurants, faced displacement in 2008; the university later recruited Black-owned tenants but gave no return rights.
districts.lesson: An anchor acting as master landlord reached full occupancy, at the cost of up-front tenant displacement and chain-heavy leasing.
districts.similarity: Medium-high on anchor dynamics; differs in scale and in Hyde Park's higher-income base.

sources.l: REBusiness, sale headline only (not opened), date unverified

districts.name: H Street NE
districts.stock: Early 20th-century commercial buildings; many burned in 1968 and stayed damaged for decades.
districts.lead: The DC government, H Street Main Street, private developers and bar entrepreneurs.
districts.outcomes: Became one of the country's 'hippest' corridors within about 8-10 years; a streetcar opened in 2016; decline after 2020 with closures blamed on crime.
districts.displacement_note: Within half a mile the Black share fell from 73% to 45% (2000-2010) while median home value rose from $148,724 to $354,730; Black churches and businesses left; no mitigation documented.
districts.lesson: A Main Street plus nightlife-led revival filled storefronts in about 10 years but turned over the population, and the bar mix later proved fragile.
districts.similarity: High on starting conditions; medium on context because DC's market is much hotter.

sources.l: H Street Main Street corridor profile, uploaded 2018-06

districts.name: Penn Avenue, East Liberty
districts.stock: Early 20th-century commercial core, heavily altered by 1960s urban renewal that closed hundreds of businesses.
districts.lead: East Liberty Development Inc. (a CDC founded 1979) with the city, national retail developers and private landlords.
districts.outcomes: Crime fell 49% and property values rose 120% (2008-2012); population rose 5% (2010-2020); ZIP rents reached $1,661 against $1,256 citywide (2021).
districts.displacement_note: About a quarter of nonwhite residents were lost (2000-2021) and 200+ were displaced from one complex in 2015; about a third of rentals are now affordability-restricted.
districts.lesson: Lock in housing affordability before values jump; here values rose 120% within about four years once crime fell.
districts.similarity: Medium-high: majority-Black disinvested shopping district, but a much larger regional node.

districts.name: Oretha Castle Haley Boulevard
districts.stock: 1800s-early 1900s commercial buildings including a former department store and the 1849 Dryades Market; dozens were lost.
districts.anchor_institution: No university; cultural anchors Ashe Cultural Arts Center and Cafe Reconcile.
districts.lead: The merchants association (Main Street from 2006), cultural nonprofits, the city redevelopment authority and mission developers.
districts.outcomes: By 2017: 32 net new businesses since the late 1990s, 176 jobs, $83M+ of investment and 24 buildings rehabbed; a nonprofit built a 4-storefront incubator.
districts.displacement_note: Not measured; mixed-income and senior housing and nonprofit-owned incubator space acted as de facto protection.
districts.lesson: A slow, mission-anchored, low-displacement path: about 20 years to 32 net new businesses on a historic Black shopping street.
districts.similarity: High: historic Black commercial street with deep disinvestment, revived by nonprofit anchors; no university.

districts.name: East Passyunk Avenue
districts.stock: Ten blocks of early 20th-century 2-3 storey shop-and-flat rowhouses.
districts.lead: A politically backed nonprofit landlord (later renamed PARC) plus the East Passyunk Avenue business improvement district.
districts.outcomes: The nonprofit bought and renovated 15 rundown buildings and now owns 7 storefronts; 20 new businesses opened in 2009; vacancy below 5% in 2024 (its own figure).
districts.displacement_note: Accused of gentrification; in 2024 it did not renew a 17-year Black-owned cafe over arrears, which drew a petition.
districts.lesson: A mission landlord that buys a cluster of rundown shops and curates uses can get vacancy under 5%, but its tenant choices become equity flashpoints.
districts.similarity: Low on demographics; high on the mechanism Waverly needs.

districts.name: Station North Arts District / North Avenue
districts.stock: Includes the historic North Avenue Market, which was changing owners in 2024.
districts.anchor_institution: Johns Hopkins University (funded the 2024 roadmap through Central Baltimore Partnership).
districts.lead: State Arts & Entertainment District from 2002; Central Baltimore Partnership commissioned a 2024 economic roadmap with JHU money. Thin supplementary record.
districts.outcomes: Home values rose after designation; no storefront vacancy outcomes found.
districts.displacement_note: An interview study found 'some gentrification', artists most at risk, and residents seeing institutions as more powerful than themselves.
districts.lesson: The nearest precedent with the same anchor and intermediary as Waverly; residents' sense of who holds power matters.
districts.similarity: Same anchor (JHU) and intermediary (CBP) as Waverly; outcomes thin.

sources.l: IJURR, Rich & Tsitsos, year not stated

districts.name: Dashilar / Yangmeizhu Xiejie
districts.stock: Single-storey shared courtyard houses (about 22 m2 per household in 2013) along a lane about 496 m long (another source says over 700 m).
districts.historic: Inside Beijing old-city protection; named a national history and culture zone in 2015.
districts.lead: A state-linked investment company with Xicheng District, launched through Beijing Design Week.
districts.outcomes: Over 600 of about 1,700 households left by about 2016; curated creative shops arrived from 2012; a 2020 second wave signed 1,103 households (46%); a featured 'Citywalk' spot by 2025.
districts.displacement_note: Voluntary cash or housing buy-outs; bought houses sat sealed and empty, pay was too low to buy elsewhere, and the only public toilet was removed.
districts.lesson: Curated creative tenants change a street's image fast, but sealed bought-out houses and lost amenities turn residents against newcomers.
districts.similarity: One curator holding many units, like Waverly's concentrated owner, but the tool was buying out residents, not shops.

districts.name: Baitasi Remade
districts.stock: About 37 ha of hutong courtyard houses (807 house numbers, 4,000+ buildings); about 70% in poor condition in 2016.
districts.historic: Around the Yuan-dynasty White Dagoba, a national relic since 1961; one of Beijing's 25 historic protection areas.
districts.lead: A state-commissioned renewal company working for the Xicheng district government since 2013.
districts.outcomes: By 2016 350+ households had signed and nearly 200 had moved; one business type per courtyard with grocers, barbers and repair shops kept; a 2024 best-practice award.
districts.displacement_note: Voluntary buy-outs of about 100 households a year were targeted; residents are hired in new shops; totals after 2016 unknown.
districts.lesson: Deliberately keeping everyday shops beside cafes protects local life, but piecemeal buy-outs leave a patchwork of empty houses.
districts.similarity: Patchwork vacancy like Waverly's, but the tool was resident buy-outs in fragmented tenure.

districts.name: Tianzifang
districts.stock: Shikumen lane houses (central block 1933) mixed with 1940s lane factories; about 20,000 m2 of factory floor was let out.
districts.historic: Never formally designated; saved from planned demolition in 2004 and 2006.
districts.lead: Artists and residents from the bottom up, later a district management committee; each household acted as its own landlord.
districts.outcomes: By 2009 300+ of 670+ households had moved out and let their homes; 216 shops in 2015; rents rose about sevenfold by 2014 and creative shops fell from 51 to 18 (2013-15).
districts.displacement_note: Residents rented their homes to shops and left, artists were priced out, upstairs residents bear noise and fumes, and many shops left during COVID while rents stayed high.
districts.lesson: With household landlords and no curator, the lanes slid into food, drink and souvenirs, the risk if Greenmount owners lease to the highest bidder.
districts.similarity: The 'many small owners, no curator' counterfactual for Greenmount.

districts.name: Yongqingfang, Enning Road
districts.stock: Arcade shophouses and big Xiguan houses from the late Qing to early Republic; before the project a third of land use (33%) was vacant.
districts.historic: Historic district since 2012; one of the city's best-preserved arcade streets.
districts.lead: Developer Vanke as master operator under a 15-year build-operate-transfer deal; the government takes it back in 2031.
districts.outcomes: Only 4 buildings (5%) were demolished and rebuilt; a co-development committee has 12 resident members of 25; state media called it a revived landmark in 2025.
districts.displacement_note: Relocation from 2007 moved most residents out; residents' snack stalls were asked to close and the developer staged 'local life' with props.
districts.lesson: A single master operator restores fast with little demolition, but without protected space for low-rent local uses it swaps real local life for an image of it.
districts.similarity: Single curator of a whole street; added from the building notes because it is a corridor.

sources.l: Xinhua, 'Guangzhou's Yongqingfang comes back to life' (in Chinese), 2025-07-14

districts.name: Yanaka-Nezu-Sendagi (Yanesen)
districts.stock: Pre-war wooden townhouses, rental apartments and temples; about 70 shops on the 170 m Yanaka Ginza street; traditional buildings fell 30% in 15 years from 1986.
districts.historic: No area-wide heritage designation found; a ward district plan was being prepared in 2017.
districts.lead: Residents and a local NPO, with ward support and private micro-developers such as HAGISO.
districts.outcomes: 60+ galleries, workshops and cafes opened over 24 years of an open-studio event (to 2017); the NPO master-leases 4 buildings and revived a 1938 coffee shop in 2009.
districts.displacement_note: Largely avoided; tourism strains toilets and space, short-term rentals are spreading, and buildings are still lost after inheritance.
districts.lesson: Closest in scale: NPO master leases of single empty buildings, careful tenant matching and resident-led events kept the street small-scale.
districts.similarity: Closest in scale and grain; no concentrated vacant ownership and no buy-to-own aim.

districts.name: Paris Vital'Quartier (Semaest)
districts.stock: Ordinary ground-floor shops in mixed-use apartment buildings across 11 sectors; the second phase's sectors held about 9,000 shops.
districts.historic: No heritage listing; city planning rules protect 32,500 shops and ban dark stores on ground floors.
districts.lead: Semaest, a city-controlled mixed-economy company owned mainly by the City of Paris and a public bank.
districts.outcomes: Bought 215 shop units (123 + 92), re-let them on soft terms, and sold 28 phase-one units to their tenants; phase two added 478 jobs.
districts.vacancy_change: Phase one -6.6% vacancy; phase two -18.7% and -9.7% in two sectors, under 4% through COVID (self-reported).
districts.displacement_note: Only shop units were bought, so no residents moved; rents were set to what each trade can afford.
districts.lesson: Closest mechanism match: buy shops, renovate, re-let below market with soft entry terms, then sell to tenants or a mission-locked holding company.
districts.similarity: Closest on mechanism; had public money (about EUR 93m) and a legal pre-emption right a US trust lacks.

sources.l: Ville de Paris press kit 'Paris commerces', 2023-09

districts.name: Seongsu-dong sustainable development zone
districts.stock: Former factory town; building ages unknown.
districts.lead: Seongdong-gu district government, with voluntary landlord-tenant 'co-existence' agreements and limits on new franchise stores.
districts.outcomes: In 2019 signing landlords raised rents 1.68% against 3.06% for others, and their tenants stayed 75 months against 56; the zone was enlarged 8.6 times in 2023.
districts.displacement_note: The pacts are not binding and district commercial rents still rose 42% in 2020-22; critics say the protected shops mostly serve visitors.
districts.lesson: Rent pacts and franchise limits suit buildings a trust does not own, but they need legal teeth to hold.
districts.similarity: A policy toolkit rather than a property model.

sources.l: Journal of Culture Contents vol.7, year not shown

waverly.vacancy_note: The Banner (Oct 2026) found more than 1 in 4 buildings in the Waverly Main Street district (29th-35th St) appear completely empty, and the city does not track long-term empty storefronts. Sponsor data on 79 frontage properties (Jul-Oct 2026): 44 occupied, 28 unknown, 4 vacant, 3 for lease, 9 with open vacant-building notices.
waverly.income_note: Conflicting figures: the project brief/proposal gives tract median family income of about 36-61% of area median (poverty 12-30%), while sponsor tract data show median household incomes of $103,750 (47 rows) and $68,569 (21 rows). Check against ACS block groups before use.
waverly.historic: Waverly Main Street Historic District, National Register listed 31 Dec 2013 (ref. 13001020): about 31 acres and 141 properties along Greenmount from about 29th to 35th St; 70 of 79 frontage properties are inside it. Waverly Main Street calls it a city historic district, but local (CHAP) status was not confirmed.
waverly.anchor_institution: Johns Hopkins University, about a mile west (30,210 students in fall 2024; JHU offices in the former Eastern High School on 33rd St); Central Baltimore Partnership works in the area.
waverly.ownership_note: Ownership is concentrated: LLCs controlled by one owner hold 11 Greenmount properties, most with empty storefronts (The Banner, 5 Oct 2026).
waverly.city_note: Baltimore city: population 569,997 (2025 estimate), 59.2% Black, median household income $62,177 (2020-24), 19.7% in poverty. Waverly neighbourhood: 3,551 people (2010) at about 24,000 per sq mi.
waverly.zoning_note: Sponsor data flag 68 of 79 frontage properties as C-1; the study block's zoning was not independently confirmed.
waverly.urban_renewal_note: The city lists a 'Waverly Business Area' urban renewal plan (2012) with a 2011 amendment; the brief's 1979 plan and its ban on new taverns, liquor stores and pawnshops could not be verified.
interventions_past: c.2005: one of seven city-funded shopping districts, with grants for Greenmount 28th-35th St; about $1M public and $3M private investment.
2004: a 60,000 sq ft Giant supermarket opened.
A Baltimore Main Streets district (one of nine in 2024).

aversion.waverly_evidence: In 2021-22 four neighbourhood groups, the benefits district, the councilmember and a state senator opposed the Dollar General at 3133 Greenmount; it opened anyway, closed in April 2025, and Waverly Main Street testified in Sept 2025 that it 'was not a good neighbor'.
aversion.law: Conditional use by the zoning board in C-1 and at least 2,640 ft from another small box (Sec. 14-335.2, Ord. 25-065, in force 2 Jan 2026); defined as 5,000-12,000 sq ft selling mostly items under $5 (Sec. 1-312); enabled by state law SB 869 (2022).
aversion.research: Caoui, Hollenbeck & Osborne (2022 working paper): about one grocery lost per three dollar stores within 2 miles, and fresh-produce buying down 4-7.4% (up to 30.4% for low-income households); no study links dollar stores to crime.

aversion.waverly_evidence: In 2018 the Waverly Improvement Association fought the Waverly Tavern licence (38th St and Old York Rd, outside the study block) over drug dealing and loitering; it was suspended for a week and fined $2,500.
aversion.law: Conditional use by City Council ordinance in C-1 and at least 300 ft from other alcohol retail (Sec. 14-336); no new licence within 300 ft of a church or school (MD Alc. Bev. Sec. 12-1605); stores in residential zones phased out by 2019 (Sec. 18-701); the claimed urban renewal ban is unverified.
aversion.research: Baltimore studies: each 10% more outlet access went with 4.2% more violent crime, worse for package stores (2018); closing 80 non-conforming stores was linked to 22 fewer homicides a year (2020); liquor and corner stores have about 25% more violent crime nearby (2016).

aversion.waverly_evidence: The Waverly Tavern, a corner tavern with a package side, was fought by the Waverly Improvement Association in 2018; police called it the district's 'most dangerous intersection'.
aversion.law: Conditional use by the zoning board in C-1; package sales only if over half of receipts and floor space are for drinking on site (Sec. 14-338); tavern (Class D) licences barred within 300 ft of a church or school (MD Alc. Bev. Sec. 12-1605).
aversion.research: Taverns and package stores were linked to homicide, assault and robbery in Baltimore (2018); closing 117 'sham' taverns was linked to about 1 fewer homicide a year (2020); bars open past 2 am raise assaults (Chicago, 2017). Notes grade this moderate to strong.

aversion.waverly_evidence: In Oct 2026 Waverly's largest storefront owner said the area needs fewer smoke shops (a landlord remark, not a resident vote); citywide opposition from council members, residents and teachers was strong in 2025-26.
aversion.law: Conditional use by the zoning board in C-1, and not within 750 ft of a school, rec centre, park or another smoke shop (Sec. 14-337, Ord. 26-116, signed 16 June 2026); existing shops in those zones get two years; a padlock law for illegal cannabis sales followed in Oct 2026.
aversion.research: A South Los Angeles study (2018) linked tobacco and smoke shops to more violent and property crime; a 2026 Baltimore report found five times more tobacco retailers per square mile in the poorest areas and few compliance checks.

food & drink|food & drink.basis: Restaurants cluster to share demand when distance rules are lifted and become more varied (Milan); drop to 0 for identical formats such as two carry-outs.

food & drink|retail goods.basis: Shop rental income rises with passing footfall and nearby shops (elasticity at least 0.25, Dutch streets).

food & drink|personal services.basis: Daily services and coffee or food share trips; only general footfall evidence, no pair study.

food & drink|entertainment & assembly.basis: Arts audiences spend $38.46 per event beyond admission, including dining; live music can attach to restaurants as a conditional use.

food & drink|office.basis: Daytime workers buy lunch and coffee; no pair-specific study found.

food & drink|production & light industry.basis: Light food processing is allowed in C-1; +1 if the maker has a shop front, -1 if noise, dust or smell reaches outdoor seating.

food & drink|institutional & religious.basis: Restaurant (Class B) licences are exempt from the 300-ft church and school rule; package or tavern licences within 300 ft of St. John's are -1.

food & drink|residential.basis: Restaurants are allowed even in residential zones, but outdoor dining beside homes is conditional and night noise is capped; daytime cafe +1, late-night or carry-out -1.

food & drink|vacant.basis: A dark storefront raises nearby property crime until it reopens and removes footfall (Los Angeles).

retail goods|retail goods.basis: Shops gain from each other's footfall; -1 for duplicate discount, convenience or small-box formats.

retail goods|personal services.basis: A daily-needs cluster such as a shop next to a barber; only general footfall evidence.

retail goods|entertainment & assembly.basis: Shops mostly close before evening events, so little overlap.

retail goods|production & light industry.basis: +1 if the maker sells on site.

retail goods|institutional & religious.basis: No distance rule for retail without alcohol; package liquor within 300 ft of a church or school, or a smoke shop within 750 ft of a school or park, is -1.

retail goods|residential.basis: Single-use commercial blocks had about 45% more crime than blocks with housing (Los Angeles); retail without alcohol is allowed in residential zones.

retail goods|vacant.basis: Store closures cut nearby business counts and jobs, partly through fewer shopping trips.

personal services|personal services.basis: Destination services with loyal clients; mild competition between identical formats.

personal services|institutional & religi.basis: Barbers and salons are allowed by right; body art next to a church or school is a -1 review flag.

personal services|residential.basis: Personal services are allowed in residential zones and mixed blocks are safer; amplified fitness classes before 7 am or after 9 pm are -1.

personal services|vacant.basis: Dark frontage lowers footfall and safety for neighbours.

entertainment & assembly|entertainment &.basis: The zoning board must weigh how many similar venues are nearby (saturation).

entertainment & assembly|office.basis: Offices are empty at night, so little conflict and no evidence of synergy.

entertainment & assembly|production & li.basis: Both tolerate noise and can buffer each other away from homes.

entertainment & assembly|institutional &.basis: Live-entertainment approval must weigh closeness to places of worship and schools; a quiet gallery scores 0.

entertainment & assembly|residential.basis: Noise cap of 58 dB(A), 53 after 9 pm, at the residential line; entertainment audible beyond 50 ft is banned; late venues raise assaults.

entertainment & assembly|vacant.basis: Dark frontage lowers footfall and safety on patrons' walking routes.

office|office.basis: Neutral, but long runs of frontage that is dark in the evening weaken eyes on the street.

office|residential.basis: Offices are allowed in residential zones; compatible but no synergy.

office|vacant.basis: Blight effects reach all neighbours; offices rely less on footfall, so a weaker penalty is defensible.

production & light industry|production &.basis: Shared suppliers and customers against cumulative noise.

production & light industry|institutiona.basis: Loud work during services or funerals would be -1; not legally restricted.

production & light industry|residential.basis: Enclosed small-scale making and light food processing are allowed in C-1; noisy or smelly work 9 pm-7 am next to homes is -1.

production & light industry|vacant.basis: Blight and burglary exposure; makers rely less on footfall.

institutional & religious|institutional.basis: Neutral; clusters of weekday-dark institutional frontage are a mild concern.

institutional & religious|residential.basis: Places of worship are allowed everywhere with design rules; treatment centres are not crime magnets compared with retail (Baltimore).

institutional & religious|vacant.basis: Blight lowers visitors' sense of safety.

residential|vacant.basis: Cleaning up vacant lots cut residents' safety worries 58% and gun violence 29% (Philadelphia trial); fixing abandoned buildings cut gun assaults 39%.

vacant|vacant.basis: Lost footfall and closure spillovers compound.

Alcohol retail must be at least 300 ft from other alcohol retail (the zoning board can waive it).
A new small-box discount store must be at least 2,640 ft from any existing one.
A smoke shop may not be within 750 ft of a school, rec centre, park or another smoke shop.
Adult uses must be at least 300 ft from other adult uses, residential districts, schools and places of worship.

rules.rule: Live entertainment must be an add-on to a restaurant, gallery or studio and needs approval with limits on hours, amplification and soundproofing near homes, churches, schools or parks.

Exterior lighting may not exceed 0.5 footcandle at a residential property line.

Daytime-only cafe next to housing: raise the score from 0 to +1.
Food maker with a retail counter next to food or retail: +1.

rules.applies_to: Housing next to a venue or church

adjacency.notes: Scores are -1 conflict, 0 neutral, +1 complement. Where the notes gave two tags (such as R/L), 'kind' uses the first one. Apply the rules after the category score; they matter more on Greenmount than the grid. Weights are a judgement: 1.0 next door, 0.5 across the street, 0 beyond the block, but legal radii (300, 750, 2,640 ft) apply in full on either side. The matrix assumes C-1 zoning; most pair cells rest on judgement.
